mainTopic: The limits of דינא דבר מצרא, the bordering neighbor's right of first purchase: the cases it does not cover, the order of priority among buyers, and who counts as a bordering neighbor.
overview: This amud is about דינא דבר מצרא, the right of a bordering neighbor to buy a field before an outsider. It opens by finishing an earlier case: a buyer who buys a plain plot in the middle of someone's land is using a trick to get around this right. Then the גמרא lists cases the right does not cover. These include a gift (unless it comes with an אחריות guarantee, says אמימר), selling all one's property to one buyer, selling back to the original owners, buying from or selling to a גוי, and selling a משכנתא to the lender who holds it. They also include trading a field up for a closer or better one, urgent sales for taxes, food support or burial, and sales to a woman, orphans or partners. A Jew who sells to a גוי is put in שמתא until he accepts responsibility for any harm the גוי causes the neighbor. Next comes an order of priority: city-side neighbors before field-side neighbors, and a תלמיד חכם before a שכן or a קרוב. A שכן comes before a קרוב, based on a פסוק in משלי. The neighbor's right also gives way to better or readier money and to a buyer who will build homes. We wait for a neighbor who must fetch money only if he is known to be well-off. Last, the גמרא covers split ownership of land and houses or trees, barriers between fields, and four neighbors with equal rights.

steps.title: Closing the earlier case: if the field has nothing special about it, the buyer is using a trick
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the previous discussion. If the middle plot the buyer purchased is not of special quality, we assume he bought it only as a trick to get around the neighbors' right.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if not, he is surely using a trick.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is wrapping up the case from just before this line. A buyer bought a plot in the middle of someone's land. If that plot has nothing special about it, we conclude he did it as a trick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this line, the גמרא said that if the plot he bought is better quality, he really wanted that plot. If it is not, the only reason to buy it was to make himself a 'neighbor' so he could later buy a border plot ahead of the real neighbors. Because it is a trick, the real neighbors can still use their דינא דבר מצרא.

keyTerms.meaning: to use a trick, a clever scheme to get around a rule
he is scheming, acting with cunning

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the END of a discussion that began before this section. It is not a new topic, so don't try to read it on its own.

phrases.english: And if not,
phrases.notes: He means: if the plot he bought is not better quality than the rest.

phrases.english: he is surely using a trick.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי לָא, אִיעָרוֹמֵי קָא מַעֲרֵים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the case discussed just before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Buying a plain plot in the middle of someone's land is treated as a trick, so the neighbors keep their right of first purchase.

steps.title: A gift is not subject to the neighbor's right
steps.stepSummary: A new rule: when someone gives land as a gift, the neighbor cannot claim it under דינא דבר מצרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: A gift is not subject to the law of the neighbor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts listing cases where the neighbor's right of first purchase does not apply. The first case is a gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דינא דבר מצרא gives the neighbor first right to buy a field that is being sold. A gift is not a sale. A person can give a gift to whoever he loves, so the neighbor has nothing to claim.

keyTerms.meaning: the law of the neighbor: the owner of a bordering field gets first right to buy
it does not have / it is not subject to

phrases.english: A gift is not subject
to the law of the neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתָּנָה לֵית בָּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new list of cases outside the neighbor's right.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A gift is not subject to the neighbor's right of first purchase.

steps.title: אמימר: a gift with a guarantee does fall under the neighbor's right
steps.stepSummary: אמימר adds a limit to the gift rule. If the giver wrote the receiver an אחריות guarantee, the gift looks like a sale, so the neighbor's right applies.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said: If he wrote him a guarantee, it is subject to the law of the neighbor.
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר narrows the rule from step 2. A 'gift' that comes with a property guarantee is treated like a sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People don't normally promise to pay back a gift if it is taken away. When the giver writes אחריות, it suggests money really changed hands and the 'gift' is a hidden sale. So the neighbor can still claim his right.

keyTerms.meaning: a property guarantee: a promise to pay back if the land is seized for the giver's debt

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that what counts is what the deal really is, not what it is called. A disguised sale cannot cancel the neighbor's right.

phrases.english: אמימר said:
If he wrote him a guarantee,
phrases.notes: The guarantee promises to pay the receiver back if the giver's creditors take the field.

phrases.aramaic: אִית בָּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: it is subject to the law of the neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַמֵּימָר: אִי כְּתַב לֵיהּ אַחְרָיוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the gift rule of step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A gift written with an אחריות guarantee is treated as a sale and is subject to דינא דבר מצרא.

steps.title: More cases outside the neighbor's right
steps.stepSummary: Three more cases are not subject to דינא דבר מצרא: selling all one's property to one buyer, selling back to the original owners, and buying from or selling to a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sold all his property to one person, it is not subject to the law of the neighbor. To the original owners, it is not subject to the law of the neighbor. If he bought from a גוי or sold to a גוי, it is not subject to the law of the neighbor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the list of cases where the neighbor has no first right. Each case ends with the same phrase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When everything is sold to one buyer, the seller does not have to pull out one field for the neighbor. When land returns to its original owners, they have an older connection to it than the neighbor does. The גוי cases are listed here and explained in the next steps.

phrases.english: If he sold all his property to one person,

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: it is not subject to the law of the neighbor.
If he sold to the original owners,

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: it is not subject to the law of the neighbor.
If he bought from a גוי or sold to a גוי,

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: it is not subject to the law of the neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָכַר כׇּל נְכָסָיו לְאֶחָד – לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more cases to the list that began with a gift.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling all one's property to one person, selling to the original owners, and buying from or selling to a גוי are not subject to דינא דבר מצרא.

steps.title: Why buying from a גוי is allowed: 'I chased a lion away from your border'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the first גוי case. The Jewish buyer can tell the neighbor that he did him a favor by replacing a גוי neighbor.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he bought from a גוי, it is because he can say to him: I chased a lion away from your border.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why buying from a גוי does not trigger the neighbor's right. It answers an unspoken 'why?'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the sale, the neighbor had a גוי living next to him, and he could not have bought the field from the גוי by right anyway. The Jewish buyer improved things for him by taking the גוי's place. The neighbor has no complaint against someone who helped him.

keyTerms.meaning: a lion; here a picture for a troublesome neighbor

phrases.english: If he bought from a גוי,
it is because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The buyer is speaking to the neighbor who wants to claim the field.

phrases.english: I chased a lion away from your border for you.

steps.triggerLanguage: זְבַן מִגּוֹי – דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֲרִי אַבְרַחִי לָךְ מִמִּצְרָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first גוי case from step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is buying from a גוי not subject to the neighbor's right?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The buyer did the neighbor a favor by replacing a גוי neighbor, which the גמרא calls chasing away a lion.

steps.title: Why selling to a גוי is outside the rule: a גוי is not bound by ועשית הישר והטוב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the second גוי case. The neighbor's right comes from the פסוק ועשית הישר והטוב, which does not bind a גוי, so the neighbor cannot take the field from the גוי buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sold to a גוי: a גוי is certainly not bound by 'And you shall do what is right and good.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the neighbor cannot force the גוי buyer to give up the field. This sets up the ruling about the Jewish seller in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דינא דבר מצרא is based on ועשית הישר והטוב (דברים 6:18). That is a מצוה for Jews, so a גוי buyer has no duty to step aside. The neighbor therefore has no legal claim against him.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And you shall do what is right and good,' the פסוק behind the neighbor's right
is not subject to / not bound by

phrases.english: If he sold to a גוי,
a גוי is certainly not bound by
'And you shall do what is right and good.'

steps.triggerLanguage: זַבֵּין לְגוֹי – גּוֹי וַדַּאי לָאו בַּר ״וְעָשִׂיתָ הַיָּשָׁר וְהַטּוֹב״ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second גוי case from step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is selling to a גוי not subject to the neighbor's right?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גוי is not commanded in ועשית הישר והטוב, the source of the neighbor's right.

steps.title: The Jewish seller is put in שמתא until he takes responsibility for any harm
steps.stepSummary: Even though the neighbor cannot take the field from the גוי, the Jewish seller is punished with שמתא until he accepts responsibility for any harm that comes to the neighbor because of the גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we certainly excommunicate him until he accepts upon himself all harm that comes to the neighbor because of the גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling on selling to a גוי. The neighbor has no claim on the field, but the Jew who sold it is put in שמתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 said the גוי buyer cannot be forced to give up the field. Here the גמרא turns to the Jewish seller, who caused the problem by bringing a 'lion' next to his neighbor. He stays in שמתא until he agrees to cover any losses the גוי brings on the neighbor.

keyTerms.meaning: we place him in שמתא, a form of excommunication
harm or damages that happen without one's fault

steps.whatToRemember: Buying from a גוי or selling to a גוי is outside דינא דבר מצרא. A Jew who sells to a גוי is still put in שמתא until he accepts responsibility for any harm the גוי causes the neighbor.
steps.confusionAlert: The שמתא is on the Jewish SELLER, not on the גוי buyer. The sale to the גוי stays in place.

phrases.english: But we certainly excommunicate him,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the Jew who sold the field to the גוי.

phrases.english: until he accepts upon himself
all harm that comes to the neighbor because of the גוי.

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁמּוֹתֵי וַדַּאי מְשַׁמְּתִינַן לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the penalty for the Jewish seller after step 6 explained that the גוי buyer cannot be forced to give up the field.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A Jew who sells a field to a גוי is placed in שמתא until he accepts liability for all harm the גוי causes the neighbor.

steps.title: Selling a mortgaged field to the one holding it
steps.stepSummary: If a field was given as a משכנתא and is then sold to the person holding it, the neighbor's right does not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: A mortgaged field sold to the one holding it is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another case to its list of sales the neighbor cannot block. If the owner sells a mortgaged field to the person holding the mortgage, the neighbor has no claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the list covered gifts, selling everything, selling back to old owners, and גוי cases. Here the buyer already had a real hold on the field through the משכנתא, so he is not a stranger the neighbor can push out. The next step brings support for this from the meaning of the word.

keyTerms.meaning: A mortgaged field, given to a lender who holds it and uses it
There is not in it, meaning it is not subject to
Because of, under the category of

phrases.english: A mortgaged field (sold to the one holding it)

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַשְׁכַּנְתָּא לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new case to the list of sales not subject to the neighbor's right, after the גוי discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling a mortgaged field to the one holding the mortgage is not subject to דינא דבר מצרא.

steps.title: The meaning of the word mortgage supports the rule
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reports that the elders of מתא מחסיא explained משכנתא as coming from שכונה, meaning the field 'resides' with the lender, and that this matters for דינא דבר מצרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב אשי said: The elders of מתא מחסיא told me: What is 'משכנתא'? That it resides with him. What difference does that make? For the law of the bordering neighbor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for the last rule from רב אשי. The elders of his town explained that the word משכנתא means the field 'lives' with the lender. The text then asks what difference this makes and answers that it matters for the neighbor's right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name itself shows that the lender already has a kind of home in the field. That is why he is not treated like an outside buyer, and the neighbor cannot take the field from him. The question 'what difference does it make?' gets a direct answer: it matters for דינא דבר מצרא.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: As Rav Ashi said:
The elders of Mata Meḥasya told me:
What is the meaning of 'mashkanta'?
That it resides with him.
phrases.notes: It's a wordplay: משכנתא sounds like שכונה, 'dwelling,' since the field is staying with the lender.

phrases.english: What difference does it make?
For the law of the bordering neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: אֲמַרוּ לִי סָבֵי דְּמָתָא מַחְסֵיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for the rule in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: That a mortgaged field sold to the lender is not subject to דינא דבר מצרא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The elders of מתא מחסיא, as reported by רב אשי, who explained the word משכנתא as 'residing with him' and said this matters for the neighbor's right.

steps.title: Selling one field to buy a closer or better one
steps.stepSummary: If someone sells a far field to buy a near one, or a bad field to buy a good one, the neighbor's right does not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: To sell a distant field and redeem a close one, or a bad one to redeem a good one, is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another case the neighbor cannot block. If the owner is selling in order to buy a closer or better field, he may sell to whoever is buying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the seller has his own goal: trading up to a field that is closer or better. Waiting for the neighbor could make him lose that chance, so the neighbor's claim does not stop the sale.

keyTerms.meaning: To redeem, here meaning to buy for himself

phrases.english: To sell a distant field and redeem a close one,
phrases.notes: 'Redeem' here just means buying a field for himself.

phrases.english: or a bad one to redeem a good one

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִמְכּוֹר בְּרָחוֹק וְלִגְאוֹל בְּקָרוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another case to the list of exceptions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling a far or bad field in order to buy a near or good one is not subject to דינא דבר מצרא.

steps.title: Selling to pay taxes, support or burial
steps.stepSummary: A sale made to pay for taxes, family support or burial is not subject to the neighbor's right.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sale for taxes, for food support, or for burial is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds sales made for urgent needs to the list. If the field is sold to pay taxes, food support or burial costs, the neighbor cannot block the sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are pressing costs that cannot wait. The next step gives the source: the חכמים of נהרדעא said such sales are done even without a public announcement.

phrases.english: For taxes, for food support, or for burial

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִכְרָגָא וְלִמְזוֹנֵי וְלִקְבוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another case to the list of exceptions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A field sold to pay for taxes, food support or burial is not subject to דינא דבר מצרא.

steps.title: The חכמים of נהרדעא: these sales need no announcement
steps.stepSummary: The נהרדעאי say that for taxes, support and burial, a field is sold without an אכרזתא. This supports the idea that such urgent sales are not held up for the neighbor.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Sages of נהרדעא said: For taxes, for food support and for burial, we sell without a public announcement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for the last rule from the חכמים of נהרדעא. They said that for these three needs, a field is sold even without the usual public announcement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a sale can be announced first so the best price is found. For these needs the sale cannot be delayed even for that. This shows the need is urgent enough that the neighbor's right will not hold it up either.

phrases.english: As the Sages of Neharde'a said:
For taxes, for food support, and for burial
we sell without a public announcement.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמְרִי נְהַרְדְּעָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rule in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: That sales for taxes, support and burial are not subject to דינא דבר מצרא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling of the נהרדעאי that such sales are made without an announcement because they cannot be delayed.

steps.title: Selling to a woman, orphans or partners
steps.stepSummary: A sale to a woman, to orphans, or to partners is not subject to the neighbor's right.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sale to a woman, to orphans, or to partners is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds three more kinds of buyers the neighbor cannot push out: a woman, orphans, and partners.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier cases depended on why the seller was selling. These cases depend on who is buying. The text does not give a reason here; it simply lists these buyers as exceptions.
steps.whatToRemember: The neighbor's right has many limits. It does not apply to gifts without אחריות, selling everything, selling back to old owners, גוי cases, mortgaged fields sold to the lender, trading up, urgent needs, or sales to a woman, orphans or partners.

phrases.english: To a woman, to orphans, or to partners

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְאִשָּׁה וּלְיַתְמֵי וּלְשׁוּתָּפֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the list of exceptions with cases based on who the buyer is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sale to a woman, orphans, or partners is not subject to דינא דבר מצרא.

steps.title: City-side neighbors come before field-side neighbors
steps.stepSummary: When there are neighbors on the city side and neighbors on the far field side, the city-side neighbors have first rights.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there are neighbors on the city side and neighbors on the field side, the neighbors on the city side come first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from 'when does the neighbor's right apply' to a new question: if several neighbors want the field, who comes first? The answer is that the neighbors on the city side do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new topic: priority among neighbors who all have a claim. The rule gives first right to the neighbors whose fields lie between the city and the field being sold, over the neighbors on the side farther from the city.

keyTerms.meaning: Neighbors on the field side, away from the city

phrases.english: Neighbors on the city side and neighbors on the field side
phrases.notes: Both groups border the field being sold. One group sits between it and the city, and the other is on the far side.

phrases.english: the neighbors on the city side come first.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁכֵינֵי הָעִיר וּשְׁכֵינֵי שָׂדֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from listing exceptions to setting priority among several neighbors.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Between neighbors on the city side and neighbors on the field side, the city-side neighbors have priority.

steps.title: A תלמיד חכם comes before a שכן or a קרוב
steps.stepSummary: When a neighbor or a relative competes with a תלמיד חכם to buy, the תלמיד חכם gets first rights.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a neighbor and a תלמיד חכם both want to buy, the תלמיד חכם comes first. If a relative and a תלמיד חכם both want to buy, the תלמיד חכם comes first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ranks who gets first rights to buy. A תלמיד חכם beats both a שכן and a קרוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 ranked one kind of neighbor against another. Now the גמרא ranks other kinds of buyers: a תלמיד חכם's claim is stronger than a שכן's claim and stronger than a קרוב's claim.

keyTerms.meaning: A neighbor whose field borders the one being sold

phrases.english: A neighbor and a Torah scholar —
the Torah scholar comes first.
A relative and a Torah scholar —
the Torah scholar comes first.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁכֵן וְתַלְמִיד חָכָם – תַּלְמִיד חָכָם קוֹדֵם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of priority rules after the city-side neighbor ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד חכם has priority over both a neighbor and a relative.

steps.title: Neighbor or relative: who comes first?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who has priority when a שכן and a קרוב both want to buy.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: if a neighbor and a relative both want to buy, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question that the earlier rules did not settle. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We know the תלמיד חכם beats each of them. But between the שכן and the קרוב themselves, the ranking is still open.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked (among the חכמים)

phrases.english: A question was asked:
A neighbor and a relative, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: שָׁכֵן וְקָרוֹב מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the one pairing step 15 left open.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a neighbor or a relative has priority to buy the field.

steps.title: A near neighbor is better than a far brother
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers from a פסוק in משלי that the neighbor comes before the relative.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: "Better a neighbor who is near than a brother who is far."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a פסוק. The neighbor beats the relative.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says a close neighbor is more valuable than a faraway brother. So the שכן's claim, which comes from his field touching this one, is stronger than family ties.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, introduces an answer or proof
A brother who is far away

steps.whatToRemember: Order of priority: a תלמיד חכם first, then a שכן, then a קרוב.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"Better a neighbor who is near
than a brother who is far."

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: טוֹב שָׁכֵן קָרוֹב מֵאָח רָחוֹק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The neighbor has priority over the relative, based on משלי 27:10.

steps.title: Better or readier money beats the neighbor's right
steps.stepSummary: If the outside buyer pays with better coins or with cash ready to count, the neighbor's right does not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: If these coins are good and those coins are weighed, the neighbor's law does not apply. If these coins are wrapped up and those are loose, the neighbor's law does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two cases where the seller may sell to the outsider because his payment is better. In those cases דינא דבר מצרא does not apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The neighbor's right only means he can step in on equal terms. If the outsider's coins are better quality, or are loose and ready to count right away, the terms are not equal, so the seller does not lose out by choosing him.

keyTerms.meaning: Weighed coins, checked for full weight
The law of the bordering neighbor's first right to buy

phrases.english: These coins are good
and those coins are weighed —
phrases.notes: Weighed coins are known to be full weight, so the seller may prefer them.

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בֵּיהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: the neighbor's law does not apply to it.
These are wrapped up
and those are loose —

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בֵּיהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: the neighbor's law does not apply to it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי זוּזֵי טָבֵי וְהָנֵי זוּזֵי תְּקוּלֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the list of cases where the neighbor's right gives way.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the outsider's money is better in quality or more ready to use, the neighbor cannot claim the field.

steps.title: When do we wait for the neighbor to bring money?
steps.stepSummary: If the neighbor needs real effort to raise money, we do not wait. If he says he will just go get it, we wait only if he is known to have money.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the neighbor said, "I will go, make an effort, and bring money," we do not wait for him. If he said, "I will go bring money," we check: if he is known to be well-off and able to bring it, we wait for him; if not, we do not wait.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא deals with a neighbor who does not have the money on hand. It explains when the seller must wait for him and when he may sell to the outsider.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying he needs to make an effort shows he does not really have the money, so the seller should not lose the sale. Saying he will just go get it is believable only if he is a wealthy man, so we judge by who he is.

keyTerms.meaning: I will make an effort, go to trouble
We look into it, we assess

steps.confusionAlert: The two cases look almost the same. The difference is the word אֶטְרַח: if he admits he must work hard to raise money, we never wait.

phrases.english: If he said: I will go and make an effort
and bring money —
we do not wait for him.
If he said: I will go bring money,
we look into it:
if he is a man known to be well-off
who can go and bring money —
we wait for him,
and if not, we do not wait for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר: אֵיזִיל וְאֶטְרַח וְאַיְיתֵי זוּזֵי – לָא נָטְרִינַן לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 18: ready money matters, so a neighbor without money on hand may lose his right.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We do not wait for a neighbor who must struggle to raise money; we wait only for one known to be wealthy enough to bring it quickly.

steps.title: Land owner versus owner of houses or palm trees
steps.stepSummary: When one person owns the land and another owns the houses or palm trees on it, the land owner can block the other's sale, but not the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the land belongs to one person and the houses to another, the land owner can stop the house owner from selling to someone else, but the house owner cannot stop the land owner. If the land belongs to one and the palm trees to another, the land owner can stop the palm-tree owner, but the palm-tree owner cannot stop the land owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the neighbor's right to split ownership of one property. Only the land owner gets the right to buy first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The land owner is tied to the place, so he can claim first rights when the houses or trees on it are sold. The owner of the houses or trees does not get that power over the land, so the right goes only one way.

keyTerms.meaning: Holds back, can block a sale to someone else

steps.whatToRemember: The neighbor's right gives way to better or readier money, and in split ownership only the land owner has the first right to buy.

phrases.english: Land belonging to one and houses belonging to another —
the land owner can stop the house owner,
phrases.notes: "Stop" means he can claim to buy first when the houses are sold.

phrases.aramaic: מָרֵי בָּתֵּי לָא מְעַכֵּב אַמָּרֵי דְּאַרְעָא.
phrases.english: the house owner cannot stop the land owner.
Land belonging to one and palm trees belonging to another —

phrases.aramaic: מָרֵי דְּאַרְעָא מָצֵי מְעַכֵּב אַמָּרֵי דִּקְלֵי,
phrases.english: the land owner can stop the palm-tree owner,

phrases.aramaic: מָרֵי דִּיקְלֵי לָא מָצֵי מְעַכֵּב אַמָּרֵי דְּאַרְעָא.
phrases.english: the palm-tree owner cannot stop the land owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַרְעָא דְּחַד וּבָתֵּי דְּחַד – מָרֵי אַרְעָא מְעַכֵּב אַמָּרֵי בָּתֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of neighbor-right rules with a new case of split ownership.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The land owner has first rights over houses or trees on his land; their owner has no first rights over the land.

steps.title: Building homes beats farming
steps.stepSummary: If one buyer wants the land for houses and the neighbor wants it for planting, the builder wins, and דינא דבר מצרא does not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: Land for houses versus land for planting: settling the land is preferred, and the neighbor's right to buy first does not apply here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new rule: a buyer who will build houses on the land beats a neighbor who only wants to farm it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the neighbor can force the buyer out and take the land himself. Here a stronger value wins: ישוב, settling the land with homes. So the seller may sell to the builder even if the farmer is the neighbor.

keyTerms.meaning: Settlement; making land lived-in by building homes
The law giving the bordering neighbor first right to buy

steps.confusionAlert: This does not cancel the neighbor's right in general. It is one exception, for when the outside buyer wants to build homes.

phrases.english: Land for houses
and land for planting:
phrases.notes: The case is two buyers: one wants to build houses, and the other, the neighbor, wants to plant.

phrases.english: settlement is preferred,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: and it is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַרְעָא לְבָתֵּי וְאַרְעָא לְזַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another exception to the neighbor's right, after the earlier exceptions about coins, timing and land versus houses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Building homes takes priority over farming, so the neighbor's right does not apply against a buyer who will build.

steps.title: A barrier between the fields
steps.stepSummary: If a rocky ridge or row of palms separates the fields, the neighbor keeps his right only if even one furrow can reach the field for sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a rocky ridge or a row of palm trees separates the fields, we check: if he can bring in even one furrow, the neighbor's right applies. If not, it does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether a neighbor still counts as a 'bordering' neighbor when something physical stands between the two fields.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is practical: can the neighbor's plowing actually connect to the other field? If even one furrow fits through, the fields really touch, so the right stays. If the barrier fully cuts them off, he is not truly a bordering neighbor.

keyTerms.meaning: A furrow made by a plow

phrases.english: If a rocky ridge separated the fields
or a row of palm trees,
we look:
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'I look' (round brackets); the corrected wording in square brackets says 'we look.' Same meaning either way.

phrases.english: if he can bring into it
even one furrow,
phrases.notes: He means: is there a gap wide enough for the neighbor's plow line to cross into the field for sale?

phrases.aramaic: אִית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא,
phrases.english: it is subject to the law of the bordering neighbor,
and if not,

phrases.aramaic: לֵית בַּהּ מִשּׁוּם דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא.
phrases.english: it is not subject to the law of the bordering neighbor.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַפְסֵיק מְשׁוּנִּיתָא אוֹ רִיכְבָּא דְּדִיקְלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from who wins between buyers to defining who counts as a bordering neighbor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A barrier removes the neighbor's right only if not even one furrow can connect the two fields.

steps.title: Four neighbors around one field
steps.stepSummary: If four neighbors border a field, whoever buys first keeps it. If they all come together, they divide it diagonally.
steps.simpleTranslation: With four bordering neighbors: if one of them bought first, his purchase stands. If they all came at the same time, they divide it diagonally.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא handles a field surrounded by four neighbors, each with an equal right to buy it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since all four have the same right, none can push out another who already bought, so the first buyer keeps it. If they come together, cutting the field from corner to corner gives each one the triangle next to his own land.

keyTerms.meaning: His purchase is a valid purchase

steps.whatToRemember: The neighbor's right has limits: building homes beats farming, a full barrier cancels it, and between equal neighbors the first buyer wins, or they split the field diagonally.

phrases.english: These four bordering neighbors,
where one of them went first and bought it,
his purchase is a valid purchase.
And if they all came at the same time,
they divide it diagonally.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי אַרְבָּעָה בְּנֵי מִצְרָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining a single bordering neighbor, the גמרא handles several neighbors with equal rights.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Among equal neighbors, the first buyer keeps the field. If they all come at once, it is split diagonally.
